original_summary: Quadrille is a four-player, 40-card trick-taking game descended from Ombre. Bidding decides a Taker, who names trump and either calls a King, making that King's holder a concealed partner, or plays solo against three. The permanent black-Ace trumps (Spadille, Baste) and the trump-dependent Manille top the trump order, and stakes are settled by whether the Taker's side reaches six tricks.

review.evidence: Original and previous variation alike. Always Pass hands the priority seat a forced contract and leaves the passer a defender who loses d whenever a strong Taker makes it. Always bidding 5 gets codille, -5 per side member, on most hands. Always calling the same seat ignores the hand. The priority seat rotates evenly, each seat twice in 8 hands, so no seat has a built-in edge. Four players means one rival's gain is not simply another's loss.

Card luck exists per hand, but over 8 hands a player chooses when to bid, how high, whom to call, and how to lead and follow. A bad hand can pass and defend, and a good hand can be underbid or squandered. Inferring the concealed partner and counting the 20 cards are both learnable skills.

A weak player still scores by passing and defending sensibly. A strong player can improve indefinitely: bid calibration against remise/codille risk, choosing a call versus a solo (solo pays 3d), reading bids to find who holds the top trumps, signalling to a partner who knows it while opponents do not, and card-counting a fully dealt 20-card pack.

Three layers of hidden information must be inferred. Hands are private. In a call, partner identity is known only to the Taker and the partner. Defenders cannot tell whether a hand is a solo. Bids and plays are the only evidence. Planning spans 5 tricks per hand and 8 hands of score race.
Trick winners follow from card power. Hand results follow from tricks versus contract. Final scores and the winner are pure arithmetic, with tricks won as tiebreak.

The original has 40 cards, 10-card hands, Matador refusals, multiple contract levels and fish stakes, which is far too long. The previous variation was close but failed the build. Trick resolution was specified as six card categories evaluated per card through branching logic, which does not fit a 20-step round without a lookup operation. Its complexity report was also wrong: it declared 2 hidden elements while it had 3 (hands, partner, hidden T). Its claimed 18 steps was not backed by a step list.

problems: P1 Step budget: the previous variation resolved each trick through per-card category branching (Spadille / Manille / Baste / other trump / led suit / other) for 4 cards, plus argmax and side-count updates, which realistically exceeds 20 steps per round once deal, bid, declaration and scoring steps are added.
P2 Hand scoring was specified as 6 separate cases (made/remise/codille x call/solo), costing extra steps.
P3 Misreported complexity: a hidden running count T was an extra hidden element (3, declared 2), and no step-by-step list supported the step count.
P4 Hidden T had to be updated every trick using the hidden partner, adding a conditional hidden-state update every round.

changes.what: Encode every card as a number: code = 10 x suit + rank, with suits Spades 1, Clubs 2, Hearts 3, Diamonds 4 and ranks A 1, 2 2, J 3, Q 4, K 5. Spadille is 11 and Baste is 21. A card's power is then ONE formula applied to all four played cards in a single step: 30 if code 11; 28 if code 21; 29 if code = 10t+2 (Manille); 20+rank if its suit is trump t; rank if its suit is the led suit; else 0. The winner is one argmax step.
changes.why: Replaces six-way category branching with a single arithmetic calc. The rank codes double as plain-card power, so no table is needed.

changes.what: Score a hand in two steps: one calc for d = B-1 if T>=B, -(B-1) if T=B-1, else -B. Then one update applying +3d (solo Taker) or +d (call side) or -d (others) through per-player if-conditions.

Drop the hidden running count T. Each player instead has a public 'hand tricks' count, since who wins each trick is announced anyway. At the end of the hand, T = hand tricks of the Taker plus hand tricks of the partner, with the partner counted only if a different seat.
changes.why: Removes a per-trick hidden conditional update and one hidden element. The information is unchanged, because defenders still do not know which count belongs to the Taker's side.
changes.fixes: P4 Hidden T and P3 Misreported complexity

changes.what: Provide an explicit numbered step list, with each start-of-hand and end-of-hand step guarded by a 'when' condition on the trick number. The total is 18 steps, 4 choice steps, 16 attributes, 2 hidden elements (hands, partner identity) and 1 random draw (the deal, first trick of a hand only).
changes.why: Makes the budget verifiable and the report honest.

keeps: Four players, trick-taking with must-follow-suit and optional trumping when void
Spadille (A of Spades) as permanent top trump, Manille (2 of trump) second, Baste (A of Clubs) third, always trumps whatever suit is trump
Bidding for the right to be Taker and name trump
The call with a concealed partner known only to the Taker and that partner, versus a solo against three, with solo paying more
Made / remise / codille outcomes graded by how far the Taker's side falls short
Zero-sum stake settlement among the four players

recommendation.reason: The concealed-partner trick-taking core gives real inference and opponent modelling. With numeric card codes and a single power formula it fits the step budget without losing its identity.

variation.name: Concealed Quadrille
variation.summary: A 20-card, four-player Quadrille in 8 hands of 5 tricks. Bid for Taker, name trump and secretly call a partner (or secretly go solo), then play tricks under Spadille-Manille-Baste trumps. Defenders must work out who is on the Taker's side.
variation.rules:
PACK AND CARD CODES: 20 cards. Each suit has A, 2, J, Q, K. Suits are numbered Spades 1, Clubs 2, Hearts 3, Diamonds 4. Ranks are numbered A 1, 2 2, J 3, Q 4, K 5. A card's code is 10 x suit + rank: for example K of Hearts = 35, A of Spades = 11 (Spadille), A of Clubs = 21 (Baste). Cards are always shown to players by name and code.

SEATS AND PUBLIC RECORDS: Seats 1-4 sit clockwise. Each player has a public score (starts 0), a public 'tricks won' total for the game (starts 0) and a public 'hand tricks' count (reset to 0 at the start of each hand).

STRUCTURE: 8 hands of 5 tricks, 40 rounds. One round is one trick. Hand h covers rounds 5h-4 to 5h. The priority seat of hand h is seat ((h-1) mod 4)+1, so the order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4.

START OF EACH HAND (first trick of the hand only):
1. DEAL: Shuffle the 20 cards and deal 5 privately to each player. Set every player's hand tricks to 0.
2. BID: All players at the same moment choose Pass, 3, 4 or 5: the number of tricks out of 5 their side promises to win. All bids are announced.
3. TAKER: The highest bid wins. Ties go to the tied player who comes first clockwise starting from the priority seat (that seat itself first). If all four pass, the priority seat is Taker with contract 3. The winning bid is the contract B.
4. DECLARATION: The Taker privately chooses a trump suit (Spades, Clubs, Hearts or Diamonds) and a partner seat (any of seats 1-4, including their own): 16 options. The trump suit is announced to all. If the partner seat is another player, the hand is a CALL and that player alone is privately told 'you are the Taker's partner'. If the Taker names their own seat, the hand is a SOLO and nobody is told anything beyond the trump suit. Nobody else learns the partner seat until the hand ends.

TRUMPS: The trumps are every card of the trump suit plus Spadille (code 11) and Baste (code 21), whatever the trump suit. Spadille and Baste count as trump-suit cards and as no other suit. Manille is the 2 of the trump suit. With red trump there are 7 trumps, and Spades and Clubs each have 4 non-trump cards. With black trump there are 6 trumps.

PLAY OF A TRICK:
- On the first trick of a hand the Taker leads. Afterwards the winner of the previous trick leads.
- The leader chooses any card from their hand. It is removed from the hand and shown to all.
- The led suit L is the trump suit if the led card is Spadille, Baste or any trump-suit card. Otherwise it is the led card's suit.
- The other three players then each choose a card from their hand at the same moment. A player holding any card of suit L (counting Spadille and Baste as trump suit) must play one. A player holding none may play any card. Illegal choices are not accepted.

CARD POWER: For each of the four played cards, with t the trump suit number:
- Spadille (11): 30.
- Manille (code 10t+2): 29.
- Baste (21): 28.
- Other card of the trump suit: 20 + rank (K 25, Q 24, J 23, red A 21).
- Non-trump card of the led suit: its rank (K 5, Q 4, J 3, 2 2, red A 1).
- Any other card: 0.
The highest power wins the trick. Ties cannot occur. All four cards and the winner are announced, and the winner adds 1 to their tricks won and their hand tricks.

HAND SCORING (after the fifth trick of a hand):
- T = the Taker's hand tricks, plus the partner's hand tricks if the hand is a call.
- d = B-1 if T >= B (made). d = -(B-1) if T = B-1 (remise). d = -B if T <= B-2 (codille).
- CALL: the Taker and the partner each gain d; the other two each lose d.
- SOLO: the Taker gains 3d; each of the other three loses d.
- Every hand sums to zero. The partner seat (or the fact that it was a solo), T, d and all scores are then announced.

NO TALK: There is no discussion phase. All communication is through bids and cards.

END: After round 40 the game ends and the winner is decided as in the objective.

STEP LIST PER ROUND (for building):
(1) [first trick of hand] deal 5 cards to each player.
(2) [first trick] reset hand tricks to 0.
(3) [first trick] simultaneous bid poll.
(4) [first trick] announce bids, compute Taker and B with key = bid x 10 + (4 - ((seat - priority) mod 4)), Pass = 0; all pass gives the priority seat and B = 3.
(5) [first trick] Taker's declaration choice.
(6) [first trick] store t and the hidden partner, announce trump.
(7) [first trick, when call] privately notify the partner.
(8) set leader = Taker on the first trick, else the last winner.
(9) leader's lead choice, remove the card, announce.
(10) compute L.
(11) simultaneous follow poll of the other three, with the legality check.
(12) compute power for all four played cards with the one formula.
(13) argmax: set last winner.
(14) announce the cards and winner, add 1 to the winner's tricks won and hand tricks.
(15) [fifth trick of hand] compute T and d.
(16) [fifth trick] update all scores with call/solo conditions.
(17) [fifth trick] announce partner or solo, T, d and scores.
(18) [round 40] decide the winner.
variation.objective: After round 40, the player with the highest score wins. If several tie for the highest score, the one among them with the most tricks won over the whole game wins. If that also ties, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Play should be identical in spirit to the previous variation, now buildable inside the step limit. Bidding becomes a risk judgement, because remise and codille punish overbidding, while passing leaves you paying a strong Taker. The Taker must choose between a solo (3d, all risk) and calling a partner, picking the seat whose bid suggests complementary strength. Defenders must infer from bids and cards who the hidden partner is, or whether one exists, while the partner can play to help a Taker who knows them. Over 8 hands, card-deal luck is diluted and good bidding, inference and card counting decide the winner. Talk is left out deliberately, because public talk would let the partner reveal themselves and dissolve the concealed-partnership inference that is the game's reasoning content.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFF CHECK. Every outcome is zero-sum. Call: +2+2-2-2=0 and +4+4-4-4=0. Solo: +6-2x3=0, -6+2x3=0, -9+3x3=0, +12-4x3=0. Each seat is Taker exactly once, so the Taker role itself is symmetric across the game.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES. No single option dominates:
- 'Always lead your longest suit as Taker' risks remise or codille when the trump honours (Spadille, Manille, Baste) lie with others.
- 'Always force a solo' (lead a suit whose King you hold) pays +6 at T>=4, but -6 at T=3 and -9 at T<=2. With 7 of 28 cards against 21, a solo makes 4 tricks only with a strong trump holding.
- 'Always play the highest card' wastes trump honours on tricks the partner already wins.
No thoughtless policy wins or draws almost every time.

WINNER-RULE PROBLEM. The partner is whoever was dealt the King, so partnership is random. Partners then get identical results.

Model the typical case: four calls, each won by the Taker side at T=4-6. Player i is Taker once and partner p_i times, with sum of p_i = 4. Each hand's partner is uniform over the three non-Takers. Score = 2(1+p_i) - 2(3-p_i) = 4p_i - 4.

There are 81 equally likely partner assignments. Patterns of (p_1..p_4):
- (1,1,1,1): the partners form a derangement, 9 ways. This is a four-way draw.
- (2,2,0,0): 6 pairs x 2 ways = 12 ways. This is a two-way draw.
- Unique top total: 60 ways.
Draws = 21/81 = 7/27, about 26%.

Voles, remises and solos lower this somewhat, but a draw rate near 20-25% is too high. Every draw is produced by the deal, not by play.

SEAT EDGE. Seat 4 is Taker last and knows the standings. It can choose a call or a solo, or a high-variance suit, knowing exactly what it needs. Seats 1-3 decide blind.

Verdict: the draw rate is too high, and the partner advantage is assigned by the deal, not earned.

playable.evidence:
RULES. Mostly complete and unambiguous:
- Trump is set by the opening lead.
- Following suit is defined, with the black Aces belonging to trump.
- Powers are unique: trump runs 20..12 and the led suit 8..2, so a trick never ties and an off-suit 0 never wins.
- The leader of the next trick and the King reveal are specified.
- No talk with four players is a defensible choice: sides are hidden, and talk would be unenforceable signalling only.

COMPLEXITY UNDERSTATED. The step list is flat, so hand-end scoring must sit in every round as `when`-guarded steps. Count per round:
- 4 sequential card-choice steps.
- 1 step to set trump on trick 1.
- About 4 calc steps for card powers. There is no lookup operation, and power depends on trump suit, led suit, rank and black-Ace status. Encoding a 28-card table in one calc per card is doubtful.
- 1 step for the trick winner.
- 1 step to credit the side and set the next leader.
- 1 step for the King/partner reveal.
- 1 deal step (shuffle and 4 private hands) on hand-start rounds.
- 8 scoring steps: call and solo across 4 T ranges.
That is at least 21 steps before must-follow legality checks. This exceeds steps_per_round 20, against the stated 16.

ATTRIBUTES. Also plausibly over the stated 13:
- 4 scores, 4 secret sides, trump, led suit, leader, Taker-side tricks and contract type already make 13.
- Current-trick cards and powers add up to 4 more.

The stated figures are not credible, and the design as written exceeds the platform limits.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT DECIDES THE WINNER.
- There are only 4 deals of 7 cards.
- Each player's single Taker hand depends on being dealt trump honours. Spadille, Manille and Baste are 3 of 28 cards. P(a given player holds none) = C(25,7)/C(28,7) = 480700/1184040, about 41%.
- The partner is fixed by who holds the King of trump. The Taker cannot know this, and choosing the suit only partly steers it.

WITH EQUAL GOOD PLAY. In the model above, with every Taker side winning, the ranking is exactly 4p_i - 4. It is set entirely by how often the deal made a player someone's partner, so the winner or a draw is decided by the deal alone.

WHERE SKILL COUNTS. There is real inference:
- reading the hidden partner from play;
- choosing a call or a solo;
- card play and counting the 28 cards.
This shifts individual tricks, but over 28 tricks it rarely overturns a strong versus weak Taker hand, or the random partner count.

ESTIMATE. Chance decides roughly 60% or more of results. A good reasoner is favoured, but not clearly, and with equal skill the deal decides.

required_changes: Reduce dependence on random partnership. Either fix partnerships for the whole game (seats 1+3 vs 2+4, with a team-total winner), or let the Taker name the partner seat directly while the partner's hand stays hidden. Partner status then becomes a decision, not a deal outcome.

Cut luck per deal and add hands. For example, use 5 tricks per hand x 8 hands = 40 rounds, so each player is Taker twice and deals average out. Alternatively, replay the same deal with seats rotated (duplicate-style) and compare scores.

Add a bidding step so that strong hands earn the right to take. For example, a simultaneous numeric bid of target tricks at each hand start: the highest bid becomes Taker and must reach the bid. Taking then rewards hand evaluation, not seat rotation.

Lower the draw rate. Break ties for the highest total by most hands won as Taker, then by total tricks won, all kept as game numbers. Or add +1 per trick won by a player's side, so totals rarely coincide.
Remove seat 4's informational edge. Randomise and reveal the Taker order at the start, or rotate the order across 8 hands so that each seat is last Taker once.

Restate the complexity honestly and fit it within 20 steps: encode each card as a number so that power is one calc per card (trump flag x 20 + rank code, with a led-suit flag); collapse the 8 scoring cases into one or two calc steps using a multiplier (1 for call, 3 for solo) and an outcome value from T; list the real per-round step and attribute counts.

balanced.evidence: PAYOFF TABLE, all hands zero-sum. d is B-1 if made, -(B-1) on remise, -B on codille. B=3: made +2, remise -2, codille -3. B=4: +3, -3, -4. B=5: +4, -4, -5. In a CALL the Taker and partner each get d and the defenders each get -d (2d-2d=0). In a SOLO the Taker gets 3d and each defender -d (3d-3d=0). So the ordering is consistent: higher contracts carry higher stakes and asymmetric risk, and solo pays triple for facing three opponents with 5 of 20 cards. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES. (1) Always bid 5: the player wins the auction almost every hand, since ties go by clockwise order from the rotating priority seat. Calling the second-highest bidder, the side needs all 5 tricks, which is rare with 10 of 20 cards. T<=3 is codille at -5 each, so the policy bleeds heavily and loses to sensible play and usually to random play. (2) Always pass: the player is Taker only when all pass and it holds priority (forced B=3), so it is mostly a defender losing d whenever the opponents make. It never gains control and loses to sensible players. Against random bidders it is not safe either, because they make contracts against it. (3) Always bid 3: the player becomes Taker whenever nobody bids higher and the tie order favours it. It wins with B=3 only if P(make) > ~0.55. That roughly balances with a strong hand but loses with weak hands, which sensible players avoid by passing, so it is not dominant. (4) Always solo: making 3 of 5 alone with 5 cards needs most of Spadille, Manille and Baste. Otherwise it is -6 or -9, so it loses badly. (5) Always lead your highest card: this wastes trumps and loses to players who count trumps. No bid, declaration or card option is strictly better regardless of the others, and no policy never loses under the winner rule (highest score, then tricks won). SEAT EDGE: priority goes 1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4, so each seat has priority, tie precedence and the forced all-pass contract exactly twice in 8 hands. Leading trick 1 belongs to the Taker, not a seat. Seats are symmetric. Everyone can win: one made solo (+6 to +12) or two made calls can top the table.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete and finite: 40 rounds, all 20 cards dealt, follow-suit defined including Spadille and Baste on trump leads, power values distinct so there are no ties, the hidden partner told privately, solo not announced, and the winner computed from public scores with tricks won as tiebreak. Choices per round are at most 4 (bid poll, declaration, lead, simultaneous follow poll), and the simultaneous follow is correctly a poll. There is one random draw per hand. No talk is justified: the game is about concealed partnership, so signalling by bids and cards is the reasoning content, and players have bids, trump and cards to infer from rather than guessing blind. PROBLEM 1, step budget. The engine has no lookup operation (a 9-cell rps matrix costs ~13 steps). Each trick must compute power for 4 cards, and each card falls into one of 6 trump-dependent or led-suit-dependent categories: Spadille, Manille (which depends on trump), Baste, other trump, card of the led suit, other. That is ~20+ conditional operations, plus argmax and winner seat, plus updating tricks won and T. Every first round also needs the deal, the bid poll, Taker resolution with a rotating tie order, the declaration and private notifications. Every fifth round adds made/remise/codille x call/solo scoring (6 cases), the partner reveal and the T reset. The claimed 18 steps is not credible as specified; realistically it is well above 20. PROBLEM 2, misstated complexity. The hidden elements are hands, partner identity and the hidden count T, which is 3, not the declared 2. That is within the limit but misreported.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance is substantial. There are 8 deals of 5-card hands, swings run up to +/-12 per solo hand, and the forced all-pass B=3 can stick a weak priority seat. Simultaneous following removes positional card play. Estimated luck share is ~40-50% of the outcome. Skill still clearly matters. Bidding: weak hands pass and lose only d, while strong hands take and choose trump. Partner selection: calling the seat with the second-highest public bid is an inference. Solo versus call: this is a risk calculation. Defenders must infer who the hidden partner is, or whether it is a solo, from bids and cards. Trump counting matters too (6 or 7 trumps, with Spadille, Manille and Baste tracked). The deal is not a hidden-type win condition: with equal good play the result still depends on interacting bid and partner decisions, and a better reasoner avoids codilles and exploits overbidders. So good play can overcome the deal over 8 hands.

required_changes: Make trick resolution fit the step budget: encode each card as a number (suit*10+rank) and compute each card's power with ONE arithmetic calc formula, for example power = isTrump*(20+trumpRank) + (1-isTrump)*(suit==led)*plainRank, with Spadille, Manille and Baste given fixed trumpRank values. Then use one max/argmax step. Alternatively, store a precomputed power list for the hand at declaration as a game list and read it by index.
Collapse hand scoring into one formula step for d (made/remise/codille) and one conditional update per player using 'when solo' / 'when call' guards.
Submit a step-by-step list showing the per-round total is at most 20.
Correct the declared hidden_elements to 3 (hands, partner identity, T).

balanced.evidence: PAYOFF TABLE (side delta d per hand; call: Taker and partner +d each, the other two -d each; solo: Taker +3d, the others -d each). B=3: made (T>=3) +2, remise (T=2) -2, codille (T<=1) -3. B=4: +3, -3 (T=3), -4 (T<=2). B=5: +4, -4 (T=4), -5 (T<=3). Solo B=3 pays the Taker +6, -6 or -9. Each hand sums to zero: call d+d-d-d=0, solo 3d-3d=0. A higher bid adds only +1 to the gain but adds +1 to the remise loss and +1 to the codille loss. Bidding high therefore buys priority at a real risk, so the bid is a genuine trade-off. TRICK ARITHMETIC: the card powers are distinct in every case. Trump powers are 30, 29 and 28, then 20+rank, which is 21, 23, 24 or 25; the 2 of trump is always Manille. Non-trump cards of the led suit score rank 1-5, unique within a suit. The led card always has power >=1, so the 0-power cards can never win a trick, and the claim 'ties cannot occur' holds. The trump counts are also right: red trump gives 5+2=7 trumps; black trump gives 5+1=6, with the other black suit holding 4 cards (codes 22-25 or 12-15). THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the WINNER RULE (highest score wins). (a) Always Pass (the first option): this player is a defender in almost every hand and loses 2-4 whenever a sensibly chosen contract is made. They become Taker only on their own 2 priority hands when everyone passes, and then hold a contract-3 obligation on a random hand. Against sensible bidders who take the contract only with trump length, they finish below the takers, so the policy loses. Against random players it can win sometimes, by gaining when random takers fail, but it does not win or draw almost every time. (b) Always bid 5 (the last option): the side must win 5 of 5 tricks. With a random partner and a random hand that is rare, and each failure costs -4 or -5 (-12 or -15 when solo), so the policy loses heavily. (c) Always bid 3: this player becomes Taker on weak hands and fails at -2 or -3, so they lose to selective bidders. (d) Always lead or follow with the first legal card: they waste trumps and the lead, so they lose. No policy never loses, and no option is strictly dominant. SEAT EDGE: the priority seat rotates 1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4, so each seat holds priority twice; the tie-break key bid*10+(4-offset) favours priority evenly over the game. The Taker's first lead is earned by winning the bid. INFORMATION: the partner knows they are the partner, while the defenders do not. This is symmetric in expectation because every seat is equally likely to occupy each role. Every seat can realistically win. The only cooperation is the temporary call partnership, whose members gain identical amounts, so no 'never behind' option destroys it.

playable.evidence: COMPLETENESS: the rules fully specify the following. The pack and codes: 20 cards, all dealt 5 each. The bid: a simultaneous poll with tie-break key bid*10+(4-((seat-priority) mod 4)); Pass=0 gives a key of at most 4, below 30, so an all-pass correctly falls to the priority seat with B=3. The declaration: 16 options, solo included. The lead, the led suit L, and the follow-suit obligation with Spadille and Baste counted as trump. The power formula, the argmax, the hand scoring, and the final tie-break (tricks won, then draw). I found no unhandled situation. FINITE: exactly 40 rounds, decided by arithmetic on stored scores and trick counts; no judge, board or clock is needed. LIMITS: 18 steps (<=20); 4 choice steps: bid poll, declaration, lead, follow poll (<=4); about 15-16 attributes, within 20. These are: per player score, tricks won, hand tricks, bid, played card and power; per game t, partner, Taker, B, priority, last winner, L, T and d. Hidden elements are 2 (hands and the partner identity, <=3); random draws are 1 per round (the deal, only on the first trick); rounds are 40 (<=40). ENGINE: the following are all supported or have workarounds. Hidden hands; private notification over the private channel; simultaneous polls with a legality check; conditional scoring with when/if. The deal uses the shared_deck_draw workaround (remove/append), and argmax over 4 powers uses calc. The deal may need several operations, but steps 1-2 run only on first tricks and there are 2 spare steps. The three followers choose at the same moment, as the platform requires. TALK: no talk phase, with 4 players. The sides are opposed and the partner is concealed, so talk would invite bluffing. Players are not left only guessing, however. Simultaneous bids reveal strength (a losing high bidder is a likely partner), and each trick shows all four cards, so with all 20 cards dealt, card counting and partner inference are possible. Omitting talk fits the traditional no-table-talk form and keeps the concealment meaningful. LATE ROUNDS: there is no safe late option. Passing still exposes a player to -d as a defender, and an all-pass forces the priority seat to take the contract, so play still matters in the final hand.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: WHAT DECIDES IT: the deal sets hand strength. Skill then acts at five points. (1) Selective bidding: take contracts only with trump length or top trumps. Opting out is possible except in a forced all-pass, about 2 hands per seat at most. (2) Choosing trump and a partner from the public simultaneous bids, for example by naming the other bidder of 3. (3) Choosing call or solo, which pays 3x on a strong hand. (4) Inferring the hidden partner from bids and the cards played. (5) Card counting: all 20 cards are in play, so remaining holdings become deducible as tricks fall, which guides leads and follow-suit discards. CHANCE ESTIMATE: with only 8 deals among 4 players, variance is substantial; perhaps 40-50% of single-game outcomes are swung by the deal. But bad hands can be passed, and contract failures by poor bidders cost -2 to -15. Over 8 hands, a player who bids selectively and counts cards should clearly outscore random or careless bidders. EQUAL GOOD PLAY: when all players play well, results depend on how the good play meets the deals: who wins the tied bid, how partners are chosen, and how well concealment is read. No single hidden type fixes the winner. The deal adds variety, and good play can overcome it, which the criterion allows.
